spatial_claims.claim: C is an arbitrary interior point of segment AB, so C lies between A and B on line AB
BC is a segment of the line AB
AB is cut at C into segments AC and CB; BC is the uncut line in the application of Prop 2.1
R(BC,BC) is a rectangle whose sides both equal BC, hence a square on BC

configuration_map: Three collinear points A, C, B with C between A and B on line AB. No auxiliary points are constructed. The proof works entirely with rectangles and squares formed by the segments AC, CB, and AB. Step 1 establishes C between A and B. Step 2 uses this to apply 2.1, decomposing the rectangle R(AB,BC) into R(AC,BC) + R(BC,BC). Step 3 identifies R(BC,BC) as the square on BC. Step 4 performs algebraic substitution. No point changes position or role throughout the proof.
pass_reason: The proof is essentially algebraic, applying Prop 2.1 as a rectangle-area identity and performing substitution. The only spatial content is the trivially consistent claim that C divides AB into two segments (AC and CB). No angle decompositions, no interior/exterior point arguments, no ray-betweenness claims, and no non-trivial geometric constructions appear. All spatial claims are mutually consistent.
